$comment: Gemfall beat 7, the Collection's chapter 7 (docs/campaigns/gemfall.md, 7H). Defines facet_caravan, which 07r and 07l also grant. Summit: scene_tree_line's two choices set climbed_the_mountain or walked_away; the lost-fight setback sets climbed_the_mountain. Cult and clock are both decided once, at scene_tamsins_offer: sell (funded_the_break + clock_late), refuse (refused_the_cult), or hand the stones back (refused_the_cult + clock_steady). The setback path never reaches that scene and sets clock_late itself. The Walk is the Collection's own exit from the campaign, and it lives here: after the tree line a walking party plays the epilogue in this chapter (the walk_ scenes) and its endings carry endsCampaign, so the campaign completes without a chapter 8. A walking party never enters the mountain. Pacing episodes on the spine (the price board, the rival collector, the mosshorn calf, the humming night, the checkpoint, the boy on the milestone, the bend approach, Professor Tidewell, the dawn bell) set only chapter-local flags and leave cult, clock and the Walk untouched.
title: The Collection

plate.narration: At the Pinch, buyers crane their necks toward the next caravan. A dragonling climbs her ladder for a better look. The bend ahead is crowded already. Getting there first will take more than a loud voice.

objectives.label: Won the Caravan Stone at the worst bend
Gave a stone back, even though nobody made you
Saw that the gem deposit was really a crab

goal.text: Beat three other crowds to the caravan's loudest stone at the worst bend.

steps.label: Race the other crowds for stones

facet_caravan.name: The Caravan Stone
facet_caravan.text: The masterpiece stone of the fattest caravan. It hums so loud the mules wear earmuffs.

scene_like_weather.narration: The realm reads you now. Hedges grow slower as you pass. A mosshorn on the ridge sniffs your packs and quietly leaves. The warrens go silent around you, and the silence follows you like a dog nobody is feeding. Up ahead, every road funnels into the Pinch, one gap between two red hills. Finish the collection, you told Pellam. So here is the plan. Beat three other crowds to the caravan's loudest stone at the worst bend. The caravan gets there tomorrow.

choices.label: Listen to what the silence is saying

scene_like_weather_listen_silence.narration: Your bigfoot stops and listens to the silence the way other people listen to a song. It has a shape. It is a circle, a mile wide, and you are standing in the exact middle of it. "They're not frightened of us," your bigfoot says. "They're frightened of what we've got." The silence agrees.

scene_price_board.narration: At the mouth of the Pinch stands a price board as tall as a house. A dragonling girl called Bryony is up a ladder with a stick of chalk, rubbing out numbers and writing bigger ones every time the ground shrugs. Every gem-buyer on the road is staring up at it. So is your pack, which has started humming along.

variants.text: Bryony looks down at your packs from her ladder and tilts her head. "Humming pebbles," she says kindly. "Everybody starts with those."
Bryony squints at your packs and counts on her chalky fingers. "Only {facets} of the big ones," she says. "Well. Everybody starts somewhere."
Bryony takes one look at your packs, and her chalk snaps clean in half. "Nobody has {facets}," she whispers. Then she climbs to the very top of her board and starts a new column just for you.

choices.label: Do the sums in your head. You came north for this.
Risk reading the changing prices at a glance

check_price_board.prompt: Read a price board that changes every time the ground shrugs

onSuccess.narration: Every time the ground shrugs, prices jump. But the loudest stones are the cheapest: buyers think the humming means they are cracked. Nobody here knows what you know. You do the sums, and grin.

onFailure.narration: The numbers change faster than you can read them, and a puff of chalk dust sets you sneezing. Bryony laughs so hard she nearly falls off her ladder, and throws you down a stick of chalk, for luck.

scene_price_board_ask.narration: Bryony slides down the ladder. "Everything that hums," she says. "Hessa's singers in the bark masks pay double for it. The wardens take it for nothing. And Grandmother says not to sell it at all." She looks at your humming packs. "You're the weather people," she says. "Everybody's talking about you."

scene_price_board_sums.narration: You came north to get rich, and you have been doing sums since the docks. In about four seconds you work out what your packs are worth at today's prices, and have to sit down on the ladder. Bryony brings you a cup of water, then climbs up and writes a brand new number at the very top of the board, just to see.

choice_the_race.narration: Three other crowds want the same stones you do: wardens with numbered boxes, grandmothers with knitting, and people in painted bark masks with sacks. The masks are Hessa's friends from the soup tent, the Deep Hollow. They wear them to sing to the mountain, and they want to wake it up so it can fix things, so they are buying every stone they can. You need to get ahead of all of them. How?

choices.label: Ask the wardens to let you through
Nobody knows what you are for. Use that.
Push into the camps and start trading

choice_the_race_camps.narration: You push straight into the camps and start trading. Your first deal is a stone for a honeycake, which should not have worked and did. Your second is a stone for a story about the first one. By the third deal, people are coming to find you.

choice_the_race_nobody_knows.narration: Nobody knows what you are for, so nobody stops you. A warden with a numbered box walks straight past. A grandmother nods to you as if you were one of hers. A mask offers you soup. You take the soup. Everybody at the Pinch thinks you are somebody else's problem, which is exactly where you want to be.

scene_warden_pass.narration: You told the wardens the truth, and they still trust you. A clerk stamps a pass for you and waves you through without looking in your bags. The stamp feels heavy on your hand all afternoon.

scene_grandmother_look.narration: A grandmother looks at your bulging packs over her knitting for a long, long time. She does not say "No, dear." She does not say anything at all. Then she hands you a warm bead, because it is cold up there.

choices.label: Put one stone in her knitting basket

scene_grandmother_look_give_one.narration: You put one stone in her knitting basket. The needles stop. "Thank you, dear," she says, and for a moment her voice is not the knitting voice at all. She folds your fingers round the warm bead she gave you and holds them there. "Keep it close," she says. "It remembers who was kind." Then the needles start again.

scene_grandmother_look_thank.narration: You thank her and walk on. She says nothing. Her needles click a little faster. Twenty paces on, you realize she has not stopped looking at your packs, and that she has not blinked.

scene_rival_collector.narration: In the middle of the camps you meet your first real rival. Lady Fleecewick is a sheeple in a lace collar, pushing a glass cabinet on wheels. Inside are forty stones on velvet cushions, every one labeled in tiny writing. She peers at your packs through very small spectacles. "Collectors," she says. "How lovely. I'll trade. My best for your loudest."

variants.text: She counts your packs with one gloved finger and pats the glass of her cabinet. "Humming pebbles," she says, kindly. "Mine started that way too, you know. A very long time ago."
She counts your packs with one gloved finger. "{facets} of the real ones," she murmurs. "A lovely start. Do keep going, dear."
Her spectacles slide right down her nose. "{facets}," she says faintly. She looks at her forty cushions, and for the first time ever, they look a little small to her.

choices.label: Trade her your loudest stone for her best

scene_rival_collector_trade.narration: Her best stone is pink and shy and very beautiful. Your loudest stone, in her cabinet, hums so hard that every label falls off its cushion. Lady Fleecewick does not mind one bit. "Marvelous," she says, and gives you a luckstone as well, for the noise.

check_rival_collector.prompt: Out-talk a sheeple who has been collecting since before you were born

onSuccess.narration: You admire her cabinet so knowledgeably that she goes pink to the tips of her wool. In the end she will not trade at all. She gives you a luckstone, just for the conversation, and asks you to write.

onFailure.narration: You haggle hard. She haggles harder. By the end you have traded nothing, agreed to everything, and promised to visit her cabinet at home, which apparently has a room of its own. She seems delighted.

scene_rival_collector_pride.narration: Lady Fleecewick takes off her spectacles, cleans them, puts them back on, and looks again. Then she sits down very suddenly on her own cabinet. "Oh my," she says. "Oh my, oh my." She does not offer to trade after that. She only asks, very politely, whether she may draw it.

scene_road_gifts.narration: The trading is fast and loud and everybody is shouting prices. A warden runner squeezes through with a note from Pellam, copied out of the citadel ledger: your names, and beside them COLLECT, with a small question mark. Under it he has written: STILL? And in the middle of it all, the road starts bringing things back to you: things you did on the way here, walking up the hill on their own legs, as if the whole realm had been keeping your receipts.

choices.label: A flat boat is coming up the dry creek
A MossHome runner is waving a knotted cord
A boggart is sidling up with a satchel
A boggart is sidling up with a satchel
Someone in a pointed hat is pushing to the front

scene_ossley.narration: A frog in a very old hat is poling a flat boat up a creek with no water in it: the frog from the reeds of the Great River, with OLD OSSLEY painted on the side of his boat, and the boat piled with every stone the river took off somebody this season. "Stones want to go home," he says. "We only kept them until someone was going that way." He looks at your packs for a long time. "Which way are you going?"

choices.label: Ask what you still owe him from the river
Let him pole on up the mountain

scene_ossley_debt.narration: Ossley takes a long time to answer, which is how Ossley answers. His price is not coin. It never was. "One stone you didn't find," he says. "Give it to the boat. That's all."

choices.label: Choose a stone and put it in his boat

scene_mosshome_runner.narration: A MossHome runner jogs up with a string of grumbling mules, loaded with everything the Woods confiscated from careless hunters. She counts the knots on your cord. Then she looks at your packs, and counts them again, slower.

choices.label: Claim everything the cord is owed
Tell her to take the stones back to the Woods

scene_mosshome_runner_send_home.narration: "Take the stones back to the Woods," you say. The runner stares. Then she grins so wide the moss in her hair shifts, ties a new knot in your cord, and turns the mules round on the spot. "The record will like that," she calls over her shoulder, already jogging. "The record likes a surprise."

scene_mosshome_runner_claim.narration: You claim everything the cord is owed. The runner unloads it all, every shovel and hat and humming stone, and counts your packs again as she does it, slower each time. "The record will know who has these," she says, which is what she was told to say, and jogs off without looking back.

scene_boggart.narration: A boggart with a satchel full of scribbled paper sidles up, not looking at you, and says to nobody: "Catalog. Who bought what in the marsh. Very useful, for a collector. Costs one really good sentence you overheard."

choices.label: Tell it what Dunmore shouted on the grandmother's doorstep
Tell it what Grandmother Tull said about the unused bell

scene_boggart_grandma_said.narration: You tell it what Grandmother Tull said about the bell nobody rings, word for word, including the second time she said it. The boggart closes its eyes to listen and keeps them closed for some time afterwards. "Lovely," it says to nobody. "Lovely." The catalog is in your hands before you notice it has let go.

scene_boggart_wardens_said.narration: "It hums!" you shout, in Dunmore's exact voice, pointing at nothing at all. The boggart shivers all over with delight and writes it down twice, once forwards and once backwards. "Oh, that's a good one. That's a keeper." It hands over the catalog without ever once looking at you.

scene_ford_witch.narration: It is Mother Thrum, the witch from the ford queue, with a wool sock under one arm, and something in it is ringing. She looks at your packs, and then at you, and then at your packs again. "I always ask twice," she says. "Once at the ford, and once at the mountain. What do you actually want?"

scene_ford_witch_dont_know.narration: "I don't know any more," you say. Mother Thrum's face softens for the first time since the ford. She keeps her ringing sock, and ties a songbird ribbon round your wrist instead. "That's the first true thing anyone's said to me on this hill," she says. "I'll ask again. I always do."

scene_ford_witch_all_of_them.narration: "All of them," you say. Mother Thrum does not sigh, which is worse than if she had. She unwraps the sock and puts a stone from the ford in your hands, still ringing. "Then here is one more," she says. "Mind it doesn't ring you to sleep." It does not stop ringing. Not for you.

scene_mosshorn_calf.narration: Out past the camps, a mosshorn calf has lost its mother. It is all knees and moss and worried noises. Its mother stands on the ridge a stone's throw away, calling and calling, and will not come one step closer. She can hear your packs. And the calf is standing right in the middle of your silence.

choices.label: Put your packs down and carry the calf over
Lay a trail of moss for the calf to follow
Ask the mother what she is afraid of

scene_mosshorn_calf_packs_down.narration: You set the humming packs down in a heap and carry the calf over between you, taking turns at the wobbly end. The moment you are away from the packs, the mother comes trotting. She sniffs you all over. Then she licks whoever carried the calf, very wetly, from chin to eyebrow.

check_mosshorn_calf.prompt: Coax a lost mosshorn calf along a trail of moss

onSuccess.narration: Moss, moss, moss, all the way up the ridge. The calf follows it, nibbling, and walks straight into its mother's side with a happy bump.

onFailure.narration: The calf ignores the moss and follows you instead, everywhere, like a shadow with knees. In the end you walk it all the way up the ridge, packs and all, and its mother is so cross with you that she forgets to be frightened.

scene_mosshorn_calf_ask_mother.narration: Your unicorn walks up the ridge alone, slowly, and touches noses with the mother, and she lets the calf come home. "She isn't frightened of us," your unicorn says afterwards. "She's frightened of the sound. She says it sounds like the mountain, waking up."

scene_evening.narration: Evening. Campfires pop up all along the road, and the ground keeps shrugging, a little more often than this morning. Nobody pitches a tent within a stone's throw of yours.

choices.label: A centaur relay is cantering past your camp
Listen to the singers at the campfires
An Exchange caravan rolls in, and someone is waving
Lay the collection out by the fire and count it

scene_evening_count.narration: You lay your stones out on a blanket in one long, glittering line, and they hum at each other.

variants.text: You count the real ones first, which takes no time at all, because there are none. The rest of the line is rush gems, loud and pretty and ordinary. A mule wanders over, sniffs the line, and wanders off again, unimpressed.

You count the real ones first: {facets}. Then you count the whole line twice and get two different answers, because one of the rush gems keeps rolling to the end to be counted again. A few people drift over to look. One of them asks politely where you found them.

You count the real ones first: {facets}. Then you count the whole line twice and get two different answers, because one of the rush gems keeps rolling to the end to be counted again. Nobody else at the Pinch has a line like this. People stand a respectful distance off with their hats in their hands, and nobody dares come over to look.

scene_centaur_relay.narration: The centaur relay canters past your fire and does not stop. They have heard what you are for now. "Fat caravan tomorrow," one calls over her shoulder. "We're sending it the long way. Round you."

choices.label: Call after her, the old road-people way

scene_centaur_relay_fair.narration: "Fair enough," you say. She looks surprised that you did not argue, and slows to a trot for a few paces as if she might say something else. Then she does not, and the relay canters on into the dark, and the dust settles on your humming packs.

scene_centaur_relay_old_way.narration: You call after her the old road-people way, palm up, from far off, the way your family has done for longer than roads. She pulls up so hard she skids. For a long moment she looks at you, a manticore keeping the old courtesy while carrying what you carry. "Fine," she says at last. "Past you. Once. Don't make me sorry."

scene_relay_sing.narration: The relay singers have new verses about wagons that have not arrived yet, so you can hear tomorrow's traffic tonight. Then a grandmother's runner hands you a list of caves nobody may ever dig. For a collector, it looks a lot like a treasure map.

scene_ember.narration: "Darlings! From the docks!" Madame Coralie Fenn is lashed to the top of the caravan in her barrel on wheels, waving with both arms. She remembers you fondly. She also remembers the warm red stone you sold her on the quay, your very first one. It is right here in a velvet box with a new label, THE FIRST FACET, and its price has gone up a very great deal since then.

choices.label: Buy it back. It belongs in the collection.

scene_ember_too_much.narration: You wave. Madame Fenn waves back with both arms and the barrel wobbles alarmingly on its lashings. "Next time, darlings!" she calls, and the caravan rolls on toward the camps with your very first stone humming in a velvet box on top of it. You watch until the lanterns turn the corner.

scene_ember_buy_back.narration: You pay what Madame Fenn asks, which is a great deal, and she counts it twice and hugs the velvet box before she hands it over. "I always hoped it would be you, darlings," she says, and seems to mean it. The Ember Facet is warm as toast, exactly as you remember, and it hums as if it remembers you too.

scene_humming_night.narration: You lay out your bedrolls, but nobody can sleep. The stones will not stop humming. Not low and sleepy: loud, and all together, like a choir warming up. A mule in the next camp has its hooves over its ears. Somebody three tents away shouts "KEEP IT DOWN!"

choices.label: Wrap every stone in a sock
Put the Glade Stone in the middle
Have a songkeeper lead the lullaby

scene_humming_night_socks.narration: Every sock you own, and two you borrow. The stones hum on inside them, muffled, like bees in a pillow. It is quieter. It is not quiet. You fall asleep at last with very cold feet.

check_humming_night.prompt: Sing a whole pack of humming stones to sleep

onSuccess.narration: You sing the softest song you know. Slowly the stones find your note and hum along, then softer, and softer, until they are only purring. Three tents away, somebody says thank you.

onFailure.narration: You sing. The stones love it. They hum along at the tops of their voices, and the mule joins in, and the camp three tents away joins in too, and soon everybody is singing and nobody minds about sleep at all.

scene_humming_night_glade.narration: You set the Glade Stone in the middle of the pile. It hums low and slow, like wind in leaves, and one by one the other stones settle round it and hush, the way birds go quiet when the forest does. The mule takes its hooves off its ears.

rest_lonely_camp.narration: Your camp is very quiet. Nobody else's is. The stones in your packs hum all together, low and sleepy, like a cat that is far too big. Patch each other up. Tomorrow is the worst bend in the north road.

scene_checkpoint.narration: Halfway up the north road, the wardens have built a checkpoint overnight: a gate, a long table, and a clerk with two rubber stamps. Everything that hums goes into a numbered box. The queue is very long, and everybody in it is hiding stones in their hats.

choices.label: Go round the checkpoint over the scree
Show the stamp on your pass
Have a duskrunner lead everyone round over the scree

scene_checkpoint_declare.narration: You queue for an hour, then set everything on the table. The clerk's eyes go very wide. He stamps, and stamps, and logs it all twice, keeps one stone "for the seal," and hands you a receipt. Then he lets you through with the rest. The receipt hums faintly too, somehow.

check_checkpoint.prompt: Everybody scramble round a warden checkpoint over loose scree

onSuccess.narration: Up the scree and round the gate, quick and light as goats. Nobody sees. Well. One goat sees. It does not tell.

onFailure.narration: Halfway round, the scree starts to slide, and so do you, all the way down into the checkpoint queue, right at the front. The clerk looks at you, sighs, and waves you through, because the paperwork for this would take all day.

scene_checkpoint_pass.narration: The clerk sees yesterday's stamp on your pass and waves you through without looking up. Behind you, a boy in the queue watches your humming packs go past the table untouched, and his mouth falls open.

scene_milestone_boy.narration: Past the checkpoint, a boy in a coat three sizes too big sits on a milestone. His name is Alder. He holds out one small humming stone. "Will you buy it?" he asks. "I need enough for the wagon home. Mom says the mountain is no place for us now." It is a good stone. It is a very good stone.

choices.label: Pay him a fair price for it
Pay his fare home, and let him keep his stone
Tell him about your own fresh start
Tell him you can't buy it, and walk him to the wagons

scene_milestone_boy_buy.narration: You pay him a fair price, and then a bit more, because the wagon home is a long way. Alder counts the coins three times, beams, and runs for the wagon. His stone goes into your pack with the others and hums in tune at once, as if it had been waiting to join.

scene_milestone_boy_fare.narration: You give him the fare home and fold his fingers back round his stone. He stares at you. "But you're the collectors," he says. "Everybody says." You tell him everybody says a lot of things. He waves from the back of the wagon all the way down the hill.

scene_milestone_boy_fresh_start.narration: You came north for a fresh start, too, and tell him so. Alder listens with his whole face. Then he decides something. "Then I'll keep mine till I'm bigger," he says, "and come back for a fresh start of my own." He shakes your hand like a grown-up and runs to catch the wagon.

scene_milestone_boy_walk_down.narration: You tell him you can't buy his stone, and you are sorry. Alder nods like he expected it. You walk him down to the wagons anyway, and a drover going home says he can ride on the tailboard for a song. Alder sings it. It is a very long song, and by the end of it the whole wagon is singing along.

scene_roadside_glitter.narration: Just before the bend, two big glittering lumps sit on a warm patch of road. Prospectors keep trying to pick them up, and keep coming back very quickly without them. The lumps look exactly like gem deposits. They also have legs, if you look.

choices.label: Watch them carefully before doing anything
That is a gem deposit. Grab it!
Follow the trail of tiny tied grass knots around them

check_crabs.prompt: Read what the glittering lumps are trying to tell you

onSuccess.narration: They are glassback crabs, and they are waving their claws in the most polite warning in the realm: this is our warm spot. You walk the long way round, and they wave you off like aunties.

onFailure.narration: You step a little closer to get a better look, which turns out to be exactly the wrong thing to do.

encounter_crabs.narration: The gem deposits stand up. They are glassback crabs, and this is their warm spot, and they would like you off it.

onVictory.narration: The crabs decide the warm spot was overrated anyway, and clatter off sideways into the rocks, grumbling.

onDefeat.narration: The crabs shove you clean off the road and into a ditch. By the time you climb out, half your packs have burst open, and the masks are already scooping up what rolled out.

scene_bend_approach.narration: Round the last corner you can see the worst bend, and you are not the first. Wardens are stacking boxes. Grandmothers are setting out stools. Masks are tuning something that might be a song. Far below, the fattest caravan in the funnel crawls up the zigzags. You have a little time.

choices.label: Go down and make friends with the caravan's mules
Watch which wagon carries the hum
Risk a quick climb for a look inside

scene_bend_approach_mules.narration: You trot down and walk beside the lead mules for a mile, scratching ears, taking the cotton out to whisper nice things, and putting it back. By the time you peel off, the lead mule has decided you are its favorite people in the whole world.

check_bend_approach.prompt: Everybody scramble up a crumbly rock for a look inside the caravan

onSuccess.narration: From the top you can see into every wagon. Eleven are full of pots, pans and grumpy passengers. The middle one holds a single crate, nailed shut, and the canvas above it is trembling. Now you know exactly where to stand.

onFailure.narration: The rock is crumblier than it looks. You come down faster than you went up, in a little landslide of your own, and land at the feet of a grandmother, who hands you a biscuit without a word.

choice_the_bend.narration: The worst bend in the north road: a hairpin over a long drop. Here comes the fattest caravan in the funnel. Wardens are waiting with boxes, grandmothers with knitting, masks with sacks, and you. Four crowds, one wagon, and in the middle of it the caravan's masterpiece stone, humming.

choices.label: You heard this caravan in last night's song. Be there first.
The relay owes you one. Ask them to bring it your way.
You know from the catalog who bought it, and for how much
Get the other three crowds arguing with each other
Notice the middle wagon's wheel is about to come off
Flash your warden pass and walk right up to the wagon
Slip in while everyone else is shouting
The lead mule knows you. Give a whistle.
Stand exactly where the middle wagon will stop
Offer what a loud stone fetches at the Pinch
Make the caravan master an offer

choice_the_bend_axle.narration: Your bigfoot has been listening to the silence, and the silence has a wobble in it. The middle wagon's wheel is about to come off. You say so, loudly, just as it does, and while three crowds jump back from the lurching wagon, you are the one standing still enough to catch what rolls out.

choice_the_bend_crowd.narration: Your kitsune says one quiet thing to a warden about grandmothers, and one quiet thing to a grandmother about masks, and one quiet thing to a mask about wardens. Thirty seconds later all three crowds are shouting at each other across the road, and the middle wagon is standing quite alone, with you beside it.

choice_the_bend_buyers.narration: You know from the boggart's catalog exactly who bought this stone and for how much, and you say both numbers out loud before the caravan master has finished climbing down. She goes pale. Then she laughs. "Well," she says. "No point haggling with somebody who's read my post."

choice_the_bend_relay_owes.narration: The relay owes you one, and the relay pays its debts. The fattest caravan in the funnel comes round the hairpin on the wrong side of the road, straight to where you are standing, and the centaur leading it does not look at you once. "Once," she says to the air, and is gone.

choice_the_bend_early.narration: You heard this caravan in last night's verse, and you are at the hairpin an hour before anyone, sitting on the rock the lead wagon has to stop at. When it stops, the caravan master looks at you, then at the wardens and grandmothers and masks still puffing up the road behind, and shrugs. "First come," she says.

choice_the_bend_mule_whistle.narration: You whistle. The lead mule's ears shoot up through the cotton, and it turns, very firmly, toward you, and the whole caravan turns after it. The caravan master hauls on the reins and gets nowhere at all. "Fine," she says. "The mules have decided. What's your offer?"

choice_the_bend_middle_wagon.narration: While three crowds rush the lead wagon, you are already standing beside the middle one, the one with the trembling canvas. The caravan master climbs down right in front of you and blinks. "How did you know?" she says. You tell her you looked. She sells you the crate before anyone else has worked it out.

choice_the_bend_loud_offer.narration: You offer exactly what a loud stone fetches at the Pinch, which is not much, because buyers think loud means cracked. The caravan master has had a headache since this stone came aboard. She takes your offer so fast she nearly shakes your arm off. "Take it," she says. "Please. Take the noise."

check_bend.prompt: Outbid three other crowds for one humming wagon

onSuccess.narration: Your offer is so good, and so fast, that the caravan master shakes your hand before anybody else has finished shouting.

onFailure.narration: While you are still counting, a masked wagoneer quietly steers the middle wagon off up a side track. The masterpiece stone is gone, and the masks have it.

scene_caravan_won.narration: The Caravan Stone is the size of a loaf of bread and hums like a whole choir. You put it in the pack with the others, and every stone you own hums louder, all together, as if they recognize each other. The ground shakes, just once, in reply.

scene_tidewell.narration: Everyone on the road is coming down, except one person going up: a selkie with ink on both elbows and a notebook flapping. It is the selkie scholar from the Exchange, the one who stood on a tavern table shouting that the gem-light fell upward. Professor Tidewell, says the name on her notebook. She stops dead. She listens to your packs like a doctor listening to a heartbeat.

variants.text: "Hm," she whispers. "Loud, and lovely, and not one of the real ones. Have you been collecting, or only carrying?" She winks, to show she is only teasing. Then she starts muttering about "the eighth one", to nobody.
"Oh," she whispers. "I count {facets} of the real ones in there already." She nods slowly. "A fine beginning." Then she starts muttering about "the eighth one", to nobody.
"Oh," she whispers. "Oh, you have been busy. I count {facets}." She steps back, as if the packs might be hot. Then she starts muttering about "the eighth one", to nobody.

choices.label: Ask her about the eighth facet
Lay out the collection for her
Show her the Ember Facet, your very first stone

check_tidewell.prompt: Follow a very fast-talking scholar to the end of her theory

onSuccess.narration: She grabs a napkin and draws on it, very fast. "The eighth is the crown of the seal, the stone the whole arch leans on. It isn't lying loose, it isn't for sale, and taking it would be like pulling the lid off a jar." She folds the napkin into your hand. "I only ever wanted to be right," she says. "Not this right."

onFailure.narration: She starts to explain, talking faster and faster, and then the ground shakes, and her notes fly off down the hill like startled birds. She runs after them, shouting back over her shoulder, "Whatever you do, don't PRY!" You never quite hear the rest.

scene_tidewell_show.narration: You lay out the collection on a flat rock. Professor Tidewell goes down the line with one inky finger.

variants.text: She reaches the end very quickly. "Rush gems," she says. "Loud, lovely, and ordinary. The real ones are still out there, you know, and the eighth most of all." She does not scold. She pats the nearest gem, as if it had tried its best.
"{facets} of the real ones," she says, and nods. "A good start." She counts again, because she cannot help it. "The eighth is still out there, though. The one that will not be bought."

She counts it twice and has to sit down. "{facets}," she says, and laughs, and then her eyes go shiny. "I was right, and you went and found them. I don't know whether to hug you or scold you." She hugs you.

choices.label: Make camp below the tree line

scene_tidewell_ember.narration: You hold up the Ember Facet. Professor Tidewell laughs out loud. "From the Exchange! The night the gem-light fell upward! I knew one of them came down there." She holds it to her ear like a seashell, and goes quiet. "It's humming the same note as all the others," she says. "Only louder. As if it's nearly home."

choices.label: Make camp below the tree line

scene_tamsins_offer.narration: That night a woman in a bark mask sits down at your fire and takes it off. It is Hessa, from the soup tent. "We'll buy the lot," she says sweetly. "Every stone. You'd be rich, and we'd break the seal properly, all at once, so it can be fixed properly." She sets out the money in little piles, and it is a lot of little piles. The thirty coins buy only the ordinary stones traded here. Selling helps her break the seal and makes the clock late. Returning those ordinary stones to the grandmothers steadies it. Either way, you still decide whether to climb or walk.

choices.label: Sell for 30 coins; fund the break and lose time
Return the traded stones; steady the seal clock

variants.text: Your great facets are excluded from this sale. You keep those for the mountain.

scene_sold.narration: Hessa counts out every coin with great care, and thanks you, and means it. She carries away every stone you traded for at the Pinch, sack after sack.

variants.text: The rush gems you came north with, she leaves humming in your packs. "Bring those to the mountain," she says. As she goes off into the dark, the ground shakes once, hard, and does not stop for a long time. Down the hill, a bell rope creaks against its ribbon.

The great stones, the ones the road gave you, she leaves humming in your packs. "Bring those to the mountain," she says. As she goes off into the dark, the ground shakes once, hard, and does not stop for a long time. Down the hill, a bell rope creaks against its ribbon.

scene_handed_back.narration: Hessa puts her mask back on and goes. In the morning you carry every stone you traded for at the Pinch to the grandmothers' cairn and set them down one by one, and a grandmother wraps each in wool.

variants.text: The rush gems you came north with, she will not take. "Keep those, dear. The mountain will want to hear them," she says, and pats your packs, which hum on.
The great stones, the ones the road gave you, she will not take. "Those are for the mountain, dear," she says, and pats your packs, which hum on, heavier than ever.

scene_dawn_bell.narration: That morning the ground gives the biggest shake yet. Down in the last dragonling village, the great bell's ribbon slips loose, and the bell begins to swing. Just a little. Then a little more. If it rings now, every town in the foothills will think it is the ring that nobody ever says out loud.

choices.label: Run and grab the bell rope
Climb up and hug the clapper
Tie it up with your songbird ribbon

check_dawn_bell.prompt: Catch a swinging bell rope before it rings

onSuccess.narration: You reach it in three bounds and hang on with everything you have. The bell swings, slows, and stops, one hair from ringing. A grandmother in a nightcap looks out of a window and nods at you, once.

onFailure.narration: You are one step too slow. The bell gives a single small tink. The whole valley freezes. Then a grandmother leans out of a window in her nightcap and shouts, "Just the wind, dears!" and everybody breathes again.

scene_dawn_bell_clapper.narration: You scramble up the bell frame and wrap your arms round the clapper, which is cold and heavy and smells of old pennies. The bell swings you gently back and forth like a very serious swing until it gives up and stops. Getting down takes longer than getting up.

scene_dawn_bell_ribbon.narration: You tie the bell up with your songbird ribbon, with a neat bow on top. The bell stops. The ribbon sings, very faintly, a little song about staying quiet. The grandmothers agree it is the best-tied bell in the foothills, and nobody asks where the ribbon went.

choice_tree_line.narration: The tree line. Above it, the mountain, shaking in a slow, patient rhythm. Below it, the road south, and everybody else on it, running. There is not one embermoth left in the foothills. Up, or down? Climbing leads to the Keeper and another chance to decide what the stones are for. Walking ends your journey here; the realm must face the mountain without you.

rest_the_climb.narration: You walk up the mountain everyone else is running away from. Somewhere at the top is the eighth stone, the one that is not for sale. The ground shakes under every step, and your packs hum louder the higher you go, as if the stones know exactly where they are.

ending_robbed.narration: The masks are gone, and so is the fattest caravan, and so is half your collection. The ground is shaking in a slow, patient rhythm now. You gather what is left and climb, because the only stone left worth having is at the top, and you are a long way behind.

walk_scene_tree_line.narration: You turn south. Above you the mountain shakes in its slow, patient rhythm. Below you is the green, and everybody else running into it. Your packs are so full of humming stones that you sound like a walking beehive, and a passing drover gives you a very wide berth.

choices.label: Let the Caravan Stone hum the loudest, all the way down

walk_scene_tree_line_caravan_hum.narration: You let the Caravan Stone hum the loudest, all the way down, as if it were leading. Behind you, once, the mountain answers it: a single long note you feel through your boots rather than hear. Then the stone hums on, and the mountain does not answer again.

walk_scene_realm_reads.narration: The realm reads you as you go. Jackalopes go silent a mile ahead of you. A pride of manticores walks a wide, polite circle around your camp. Even the moss leans away from the path. Everything that can hear the stones steps aside, like you are weather.

choices.label: Ask the trees, kindly, why they are leaning away
Hold up the Glade Stone and let the forest hear it

walk_scene_realm_reads_glade_hum.narration: You hold up the Glade Stone and let the forest hear it. Every leaf within a hundred paces goes still at once. Not a rustle. Not a bird. The forest has recognized the sound of its own bruise, and it holds its breath until you put the stone away.

walk_scene_realm_reads_ask_trees.narration: Your unicorn asks the trees, kindly, why they lean away. The answer comes slowly, in creaks. It is not you, they say. It is what you carry, and where it is going, which is away. The trees do not sound angry. They sound like somebody watching a cart go the wrong way and deciding not to shout.

walk_rest_switchback.narration: You camp on a switchback where the rocks are still warm from the day. Nobody says much. Share out the last of the snacks, patch each other up, and listen to the mountain grumbling behind you, far away and getting farther.

walk_scene_factions.narration: On the caravan road, a centaur relay runner called Brisk is coming up as you go down. She slows to a trot. "News," she says, "if you want it. Everybody up there is doing something." She looks at your packs. "Without you."

choices.label: Ask how the wardens are doing
Ask how the grandmothers are doing
Ask whether anybody knows what you know

walk_scene_factions_close.narration: "Does anybody up there know what we know?" Brisk looks at you very hard. "You knew," she says. "You knew and you came down." She does not say anything else. She does not have to.

walk_scene_wardens_hold.narration: "The wardens did what you told them," says Brisk. "Checkpoints on every road. Every stone confiscated and logged twice. It's working. It's ugly to watch. But they're holding." A warden wagon rolls past, uphill, full of stones going home.

walk_scene_gatherers_hold.narration: "The grandmothers turned gathering law inside out," says Brisk. "Every stone that came down is going back up, carried by dragonlings with bells on their tails. It's slow. It's holding." Somewhere above you, a very small bell jingles past.

walk_scene_news.narration: "Nobody knows much," says Brisk. "The wardens are guessing. The masks are singing. The dragon is being a dragon. Everybody's waiting for somebody to do something." She looks at your packs, then at you, and does not say anything else, which for a centaur is very loud.

walk_scene_boundary.narration: At the boundary stones, a dragonling grandmother sits on the oldest stone, knitting something long and red. She looks at your humming packs. "Take what the mountain drops," she says. "Never pry at what it holds." Then she holds out one hand, palm up, and waits.

choices.label: Put a stone in her hand
Tell her you helped pay for the break
Ask her why the bells keep ringing
Ask her why her knitting needles are shaking

walk_scene_boundary_thank.narration: You thank her, and keep walking. Her hand stays out, palm up, for a long time after you have passed. You know this because you look back, and you wish you had not.

walk_scene_boundary_give.narration: You put a stone in her hand. She closes her fingers round it and holds it against the long red knitting as if warming it. "Take what the mountain drops," she says, more softly this time. "Thank you, dear." Behind you, a small bell rings a ring you have not heard before, and it is a happy one.

walk_scene_the_fuse.narration: The grandmother puts her knitting down. Up on the mountain the bells are counting, every town at once. "Everybody knows what the last ring means," she says. "Nobody says it." She does not say it either. She just looks at you for a long time, and then knits faster.

choices.label: Put a stone in her hand after all

walk_scene_the_fuse_give.narration: You put a stone in her hand after all. She looks at it, and at you, and the needles stop shaking for exactly as long as it takes her to tuck it into her apron. "Well," she says. "That's one." Then she picks up the knitting again. The bells go on counting, but somewhere under them one small bell rings a ring you have not heard before, and it is a happy one.

walk_scene_look_back.narration: At the bottom of the foothills you turn round, one last time. Mount Red Sky glows against the evening sky. Somebody up there is doing the thing you decided not to do.

choices.label: Send word back up the mountain, everything you know
Watch the embermoths settle back on the warm rocks
Listen: the grandmother's bell, ringing the happy ring

walk_check_send_word.prompt: Get a message about the seal back up the mountain in time

onSuccess.narration: A griffin courier takes your letter straight up into the smoke. By morning, the warden checkpoints are reading it aloud.

onFailure.narration: Your letter goes up with a caravan that turns round halfway, because caravans do that now.

walk_check_last_chance.prompt: Give your best stone to a dragonling runner heading uphill, and ask them to hurry

onSuccess.narration: The runner takes your stone and your message, and runs. You never learn their name. They get there.

onFailure.narration: The runner is kind, and quick, and just too late.

walk_ending_collectors.narration: The realm holds. Not because of you, but it holds. The last bell never rings. Back home, people ask where you got all those stones, and some of them ask the troll's old question: and where is it going? You are still thinking about the answer. History files you as The Collectors, and leaves the page after it blank, in case.

variants.text: You walk out of the foothills with a pack of loud, ordinary rush gems and not one real facet among them. It is a small collection to show for such a road, and a light walk home.
You walk out of the foothills with the real ones humming in your packs, {facets} of them, and a pocketful of rush gems besides.
You walk out of the foothills with the real ones humming in your packs, {facets} of them, the biggest collection anyone has ever carried down that road.

walk_ending_not_there.narration: Behind you, the last bell rings. You are a long way down the road when the mountain shrugs, and you watch the red sky grow redder from somewhere safe. The realm goes on, rearranged, and history files you as The Ones Who Weren't There.

variants.text: You walk home with only your rush gems, and a great deal of quiet. But in your pack, one stone has stopped humming. It is pointing north, like a compass, as if it is asking whether you would like to try again.

You walk home with the real ones, {facets} of them, which is something, and something is not nothing. But in your pack, one stone has stopped humming. It is pointing north, like a compass, as if it is asking whether you would like to try again.

You walk home with the real ones, {facets} of them, a collection people will cross a river to see, and it does not feel like enough. But in your pack, one stone has stopped humming. It is pointing north, like a compass, as if it is asking whether you would like to try again.

interaction_cabinet.narration: Before you go, Lady Fleecewick will not let a fellow collector leave without a small favor. One wheel of her glass cabinet has stuck in a rut, and forty stones on forty cushions are sliding toward the low corner. "Lift, dears! Gently! They bruise!" she cries, and hangs her lace shawl over your arm to keep it safe.

interaction.cue: Everyone lift or lower your side until the cushions are flat, then carry the cabinet.
interaction.objectLabel: A glass cabinet of forty stones

onSuccess.narration: Not one cushion slides. Lady Fleecewick counts her forty stones twice, takes back her shawl, and presses three coins into your hand. "Collector's courtesy," she says. "Do not spend it all on honeycakes."

onFailure.narration: The cabinet tips, and forty stones roll gently into a heap of lace. Nothing breaks. Lady Fleecewick picks them up one by one, sighing at each, and waves you on with the shawl.

onAssisted.narration: Not one cushion slides. Lady Fleecewick counts her forty stones twice, takes back her shawl, and presses three coins into your hand. "Collector's courtesy," she says. "Do not spend it all on honeycakes."

interaction_boxes.narration: Beside the checkpoint table, the numbered boxes are piling up faster than the clerk can stamp them. "You! Yes, you! Hands!" he cries, pointing at a long shelf by the road. The boxes have to go down the line hand to hand, and every single one is humming. The top one seems to be humming a song about lunch.

interaction.cue: Catch the box, then pass it down the line.

onSuccess.narration: Every box reaches the shelf. The clerk stamps the last one with both stamps at once, and pulls a honeycake out of his hat. "For the hands," he says. "It has only been in there since Tuesday."

onFailure.narration: One box slips and rolls downhill, humming happily, and three wardens chase it. The clerk sighs and stamps the rest himself, one stamp at a time.

onAssisted.narration: Every box reaches the shelf. The clerk stamps the last one with both stamps at once, and pulls a honeycake out of his hat. "For the hands," he says. "It has only been in there since Tuesday."

interaction_hairpin.narration: The last wagons are still grinding around the hairpin, one after another, and the mountain path you want is straight across their road. The wheels roll by in a slow, steady beat. A mule wearing a little straw hat stops to watch you think. Wait for a gap, and then go.

interaction.cue: Tap when the gap between the wagons is wide open.

onSuccess.narration: You dash through the gap with a whole wagon-length to spare. The mule in the straw hat nods, as if it had timed you itself.

onFailure.narration: You step out a heartbeat early, and a wagon rolls close enough to tip the mule's hat over your head. Nobody is hurt. The driver says sorry twice, and you cross on the next gap, a little out of breath.

onAssisted.narration: You dash through the gap with a whole wagon-length to spare. The mule in the straw hat nods, as if it had timed you itself.

interaction_tidewell_knocks.narration: Before she hurries off, Professor Tidewell kneels and knocks on a rock with her pencil: a slow beat in three kinds of knock. "The mountain says it in this order," she whispers. "Watch it, and knock it back to me. Then I will know somebody besides me has heard it."

interaction.cue: Watch the knocks, then knock them back in order.

onSuccess.narration: Thump, tap, tap, rumble. Professor Tidewell writes it down with a flourish and says you may be the second person in the world to have heard it properly. Then she hands back the pencil. It was yours.

onFailure.narration: Your knocks come out a little tangled, and Tidewell writes down the tangle too. "Even a muddle is data," she says cheerfully. "Mine usually are."

onAssisted.narration: Thump, tap, tap, rumble. Professor Tidewell writes it down with a flourish and says you may be the second person in the world to have heard it properly. Then she hands back the pencil. It was yours.

scene_echo_cutting.narration: Down in the village the bell is quiet now, but something up the road is not. In the cutting just below the tree line, two long gray shapes are copying every sound the valley makes, half a breath late. One copies the valley, and the other copies the first. Tink, like the bell. Thump, like the ground. A grandmother in a nightcap hurries after you, holding up her skirts. "Those are echo hunters, dears, and they have been at the bell all morning," she puffs. "They will not let anyone through the cutting while they have a sound to follow, and your stones are the loudest thing for a hundred miles. Make them lose the thread, please. The whole valley wants to get past."

encounter_echo.narration: Two echo hunters unfold out of the rock wall, one copying the other, and both copying your footsteps one beat late. Be louder than one sound, and stronger than an echo.

scene_echo_quiet.narration: The echo hunters fold themselves back into the rock and sulk, repeating only each other's grumbling. The cutting is just a cutting again. The grandmother tucks a little whistle into your hand. "For calling a village when something copies you," she says. "You will not need it. Keep it anyway."

scene_echo_lost.narration: The echoes pile up until nobody can hear themselves think. Then the grandmother bangs two pots together, loud and honest, and the echo hunters lose the thread and slink away into the rocks. She wraps everyone in blankets and hands around hot milk. There is no whistle for anyone tonight, but the cutting is clear.

interaction_price_clues.narration: Bryony saves three chalk notes before the prices change. Read them together: a loud hum scares buyers; scared buyers lower their offers; the lowest offer is on the loud wagon. What causes what? No sums required. Bryony has chalk on her nose and denies everything.

interaction.cue: Arrange cause, response, then the clue about the wagon.
clues: Buyers think the loud hum means a crack. They lower their offers.
The cheapest wagon is the loud one, not the quiet one.

onSuccess.narration: You spot the bargain: loud does not mean broken. Remember that at the bend.

onFailure.narration: The notes get chalky. Bryony explains the warning, but the bargain column has changed before you copy it.

onAssisted.narration: Bryony reads the notes with you. You copy the loud-wagon price before it changes.

interaction_wagon_watch.narration: From the rock you see a glow under one of three wagon covers. Track it as the wagons change places at the bend. The lead mule looks up as if checking your homework.

interaction.cue: Watch the glowing load, then choose its final position.

onSuccess.narration: You mark the right stopping place. The master will find you beside the stone, ahead of the shouting.

onFailure.narration: The covers cross and you lose the glow. You can still make an offer or use another preparation.

onAssisted.narration: A driver points out each wagon as it moves. You mark the right stopping place.

voiceGuide.tone: warm, glittering, a little lonely; the land treating the party like weather, never scolding; after the Walk: quiet, bittersweet, honest; the realm is never cruel to the walkers, it just tells the truth; always a spark at the end
forbidden: calling the party greedy or bad

npcVoices.hessa: Deep Hollow cell member who ran the soup tent; sweet, sincere, makes the arithmetic sound kind; says 'properly' a lot
npcVoices.old_ossley: very few words, long pauses that are not hesitation, answers the question you meant
npcVoices.grandmother: a dragonling grandmother at the boundary stones; knits, quotes the one rule, never says the thing everyone knows
npcVoices.mosshome_runner: breathless, cheerful, counts knots out loud, then counts packs
npcVoices.boggart: talks sidelong to nobody, never meets your eye, treasures overheard sentences
npcVoices.ford_witch: Mother Thrum, the ford witch; pointed hat, dry, kind underneath; only asks one question and means it
npcVoices.centaur_relay: brisk, proud of the roads, speaks over her shoulder at a canter
npcVoices.exchange_merchant: Madame Coralie Fenn, the Exchange gem-buyer in a barrel on wheels; delighted to see you, genuinely fond, calls everyone darlings, and still a merchant
npcVoices.caravan_master: exhausted, practical, will sell to whoever stops shouting first
npcVoices.brisk: Brisk, a centaur relay runner; fast-talking, fair, says a lot by saying nothing
npcVoices.bryony: a dragonling girl who keeps the price board at the Pinch; chalky, quick, nosy, cheerful
npcVoices.lady_fleecewick: a rival collector, a sheeple in a lace collar with a glass cabinet on wheels; gracious, thrilled by any stone, never sore about losing
npcVoices.alder: a boy on a milestone selling his one stone for the wagon home; polite, hopeful, trying hard to be grown-up
npcVoices.tidewell: Professor Marrow Tidewell, the selkie scholar from chapter 1; ink on both elbows, talks fast, draws on napkins, proud and worried at once
